title: When the Clock Is Ticking
subject: English
unit: Spring 2: Julius Caesar (Shakespeare): leadership, persuasion and responsibility
source: Written for english/y8 lesson 39 ('When the Clock Is Ticking' (teacher-written explanatory article, pupil PDF))
intro: Lesson 39: Non-fiction: decisions under pressure. Read the whole text, then annotate it: underline the writer's methods and note their effect in the margin.

passage.title: When the Clock Is Ticking
paras: Under pressure, the brain takes shortcuts. First, we narrow our attention: we see the threat in front of us and miss everything around it. Second, we look for approval: in a group, nobody wants to be the one who says 'Wait.' Third, we overvalue the present: the relief of acting now outweighs the cost later.
Pilots and surgeons train for this. They use checklists, pause before key steps and invite anyone to speak up. The lesson is simple: when the stakes are highest, slow down.

These shortcuts once kept our ancestors alive. If a wild animal appears, there is no time to weigh every option; running is the right answer. But most modern pressures are different. An exam, an argument or a dare from friends rarely needs a split-second decision, and yet our bodies react as if it does.

Consider a pupil who sees a message in a group chat asking everyone to share an embarrassing photo of a classmate. Attention narrows to the chat. Nobody wants to be the one who refuses. The laugh is instant; the harm comes later. Each shortcut pushes towards the same bad decision.

The good news is that the same tools pilots use work for anyone. A personal checklist can be as short as three questions: Is this kind? Is this true? Will I be glad tomorrow? A pause can be one slow breath. And speaking up gets easier with practice.
Pressure will always come. We cannot always control it, but we can decide in advance how we will meet it.

questions.q: What is the writer's main viewpoint?
questions.a: When the stakes are highest, we should slow down because pressure makes the brain take shortcuts.

questions.q: Find two methods the writer uses and explain the effect of each.
questions.a: A three-part structure (First, Second, Third); examples from pilots and surgeons; the group-chat scenario; a three-question checklist.

questions.q: How does the final paragraph end the argument?
questions.a: With a calm, hopeful statement that we can decide in advance how to meet pressure.

questions.q: Retrieve the three reasons pressure harms decisions.
questions.a: Narrowed attention; looking for approval; overvaluing the present.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention pilots and surgeons?
questions.a: They are respected experts whose high-stakes jobs prove the remedies work (ethos).

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, explain how the writer makes the ideas clear and convincing. Use two methods. Starter: 'The writer explains...'
questions.a: Two methods (signposting, expert examples, short final imperative) with effects.

questions.q: Extend: apply one reason to Brutus's decision to spare Antony.
questions.a: Narrowed attention: Brutus focuses on looking honourable and misses Antony's threat.

questions.q: Stretch: write a checklist the conspirators should have used.
questions.a: For example: Is it just? Have we heard all objections? What will Antony do?

questions.q: Which remedy fits 'nobody wants to say Wait'?
questions.a: C) Invite anyone to speak up. Inviting challenge counters group pressure; acting faster makes it worse.

questions.q: Answer the ponder in one sentence.
questions.a: Speed helps in emergencies with training; big decisions need slow, careful thought.
